The three types of knowledge tool serves reformulating research questions in order to check what (societal) knowledge demands the questions meet. Three versions of a research question are generated, each stressing a different type of knowledge:
Knowledge about what is (systems knowledge)
Knowledge about what should be (target knowledge)
Knowledge about how we come from where we are to where we should be (transformation knowledge)

On the basis of the different versions, the most relevant one with respect to (societal) knowledge demands can jointly be identified.
why_use: When formulating research questions, researchers generally follow the standards of their thought style. Whether this answers relevant (societal) knowledge demands is unclear. The three types of knowledge tool reveals some of the implicitly applied standards and allows for jointly deliberating and deciding on the relevant question(s) to pose.
when_to_use: The three types of knowledge tool supports problem framing. It is typically used when discussing and fine-tuning research questions, but can be applied at any stage as an instrument of reflection.
how_it_works: Take as an example a joint project between a humanities and a medical researcher, in medical humanities. The agreed topic of the project is: “Visualizing brain activities to improve health of epilepsy patients”. In the three types of knowledge this topic can be reformulated as follows:
How do visualised brain activities relate to health of epilepsy patients? (Systems knowledge)
How will visualisation of brain activities improve the health of epilepsy patients? (Transformation knowledge)
What is an improved health of epilepsy patients? (Target knowledge)
thought_styles: When applied in heterogeneous teams, the three types of knowledge tool bridges thought styles by revealing their implicit assumptions about ‘good’ research questions. Perhaps the reformulation reveals that the humanities researcher is interested in how the concept of a healthy brain is influenced by visualisation technologies. Whereas the medical researcher is interested in using the visualisation to improve patients’ health. Uncovering the assumptions allows for finding a joint question or for harmonizing the individual questions.
outputs: The output is an explicit deliberation and decision on the main research question(s), on how the questions relate to each other, and more clarity about what societal knowledge demand is met.
The outcome is an increased understanding of each other’s and joint research interests.
participation: A facilitator should lead through the reformulation process.
Participants should feel comfortable with formulating research questions. They may encompass academic and non-academic actors with various backgrounds.
prerequisites: The reformulation requires flipcharts and marker pens.

Before using the method for the first time, the facilitator should practice reformulation with a few examples and make sure that s/he has understood the distinction between the three types of knowledge.
limitations: When there is no flexibility in adapting the research questions and no follow-up project is planned.

title: After Action Review
short_description: A structured reflection on what happened, why, and how to improve.
long_description: After Action Review (AAR) is a team-based method for reflecting immediately after key project events. It helps capture learning before memories fade, identify what worked, and plan future improvements.
steps: Gather the team after a major activity or milestone.
Ask: What was supposed to happen?
Ask: What actually happened?
Ask: Why were there differences?
Identify lessons and next steps.

title: Group Reflection
short_description: Facilitated collective reflection to capture lessons learned and team insights.
long_description: Group Reflection brings project members together to share perspectives, challenges, and learnings. It promotes mutual understanding and ensures collective ownership of results, which is essential in the conclusion of transdisciplinary projects.
steps: Prepare guiding reflection questions.
Facilitate open sharing of experiences.
Identify successes, challenges, and surprises.
Document key lessons and commitments for future collaboration.

title: Outcome Harvesting
short_description: Identifies and analyzes outcomes that have already occurred, regardless of initial plans.
long_description: Outcome Harvesting collects evidence of what has been achieved and works backward to determine how and why it happened. It supports adaptive learning and accountability by focusing on actual changes rather than predefined indicators.
steps: Identify intended users and uses.
Harvest and verify evidence of outcomes.
Analyze causal links to project activities.
Formulate lessons learned and recommendations.

title: Learning History
short_description: Captures the collective memory of a project through narrative and analysis.
long_description: Learning History documents the evolution of a project using narratives, interviews, and data to reconstruct key decisions and outcomes. It serves as a reflective account that helps others learn from past experience.
steps: Collect project documents, interviews, and notes.
Identify critical incidents and turning points.
Construct a narrative combining multiple perspectives.
Reflect collectively on the process and outcomes.

title: Process Mapping (Retrospective)
short_description: Visualizes the sequence of project steps to analyze how results emerged.
long_description: Process Mapping is used retrospectively to identify bottlenecks, turning points, and interactions that influenced the project trajectory. It helps participants recognize patterns and areas for improvement in future collaborations.
steps: Gather a team to map the project timeline.
Identify major decisions, challenges, and interactions.
Visualize them in a flow or timeline diagram.
Discuss lessons and possible improvements.

title: Evaluation Matrix
short_description: Compares outcomes against multiple criteria to assess project success.
long_description: The Evaluation Matrix supports structured reflection by comparing expected vs. achieved results across agreed criteria such as relevance, effectiveness, and sustainability. It fosters transparent team discussion and shared learning.
steps: Define evaluation criteria and indicators.
List expected and observed results.
Rate performance on each criterion.
Discuss reasons for differences and next steps.
